speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Can you describe the specific nature of the feeding difficulties and how long the abdominal distension has been present?

speaker: Patient
text: The baby has been very fussy, feeding less than usual, and the abdomen looks distended. Crying gets worse when the belly is touched.

speaker: Doctor
text: I see. Does the baby have a fever, and have you noticed any vomiting or changes in his bowel movements?

speaker: Patient
text: There has not been fever, vomiting, or diarrhea like a stomach infection. The baby was born at 39 weeks without birth complications.

speaker: Doctor
text: Let me examine the baby's abdomen for any visible loops of bowel or signs of tenderness. I will also check his anal sphincter tone to rule out any neurological involvement.

speaker: Patient
text: The baby did not seem to pass stool normally and the belly swelling has become more obvious. Feeding has clearly decreased over the past few days.

speaker: Doctor
text: Does the baby have a history of delayed meconium passage at birth, and have you observed any explosive stools or a distinct smell upon digital rectal examination? I would also like to request an abdominal X-ray to look for dilated bowel loops. REQUEST TEST: Abdominal_X-Ray

speaker: Doctor
text: The X-ray findings of dilated bowel loops with an empty rectum, combined with the history of feeding difficulties and abdominal distension, are highly suggestive of Hirschsprung disease. I would like to request images of the abdomen to confirm the radiological signs before making a final decision. REQUEST IMAGES

speaker: Patient
text: The abdomen still looks swollen and the baby seems uncomfortable, especially in the lower abdomen.

speaker: Doctor
text: The clinical picture of delayed meconium, abdominal distension, and radiological evidence of obstruction with an empty rectum is classic for Hirschsprung disease. DIAGNOSIS READY: Hirschsprung disease
